title: Specific Goals Beat Doing Your Best
text:
In 2002 the psychologists Edwin Locke and Gary Latham summarized more than thirty years of research on goal setting, much of it their own. The research covered hundreds of studies involving many thousands of people, in laboratories and in workplaces from logging crews to scientists, across several countries.

Their central finding was consistent. When people were given specific, difficult goals, they performed better than when they were given easy goals, vague goals, or the common instruction to "do your best." The harder the goal, as long as people accepted it and had the ability to reach it, the higher the performance.

They also mapped out why goals work. Goals direct attention toward what matters, raise effort, increase persistence and push people to search for better strategies. The effect was strongest when people received feedback on their progress and were committed to the goal, for example because it mattered to them or because they had a say in setting it. For very complex tasks that people were still learning, they found that goals to learn something often worked better than goals to reach a particular output.
lesson: Instead of asking people to do their best, agree on a clear and challenging target, give feedback along the way, and for new skills set learning goals first.
location: University of Maryland, USA, and University of Toronto, Canada
source: Locke, E. A., and Latham, G. P. (2002). Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey. American Psychologist, 57(9), 705-717.
